title: Every Cure's drug-repurposing AI gave David Fajgenbaum a multiple myeloma regimen (carfilzomib, cyclophosphamide, dexamethasone) for Joseph Coates, dying of POEMS syndrome in January 2024; he improved within a week and reached a stem cell transplant and remission
summary: An AI repurposing model proposed a myeloma regimen for a dying POEMS patient; he improved in a week and reached transplant and remission.
account: In January 2024 (Every Cure's dating) Joseph Coates, 37, of Renton, Washington, was dying of POEMS syndrome, a rare blood disorder. His heart was enlarged, kidneys failing, liters of fluid drained from his abdomen every few days, too sick for a stem cell transplant. His partner Tara Theobald emailed David Fajgenbaum of the University of Pennsylvania, co-founder of the non-profit Every Cure. He replied next morning with an untested combination of chemotherapy, immunotherapy and steroids from Every Cure's repurposing model. The New Yorker names cyclophosphamide, carfilzomib and dexamethasone, a myeloma regimen. He responded within a week and had the transplant about four months later. He was in remission when the New York Times reported the case on 20 March 2025.
purpose: Every Cure's platform was built to score about 4,000 existing drugs against 18,500 diseases to find repurposing candidates. Proposing a myeloma regimen for POEMS syndrome is that function. The New Yorker notes that Every Cure does not usually make recommendations for individual patients.
system: Every Cure drug-repurposing AI platform (an early version of its algorithms scoring drugs against diseases)
developer: Every Cure (co-founded by David Fajgenbaum, University of Pennsylvania)
deployer: David Fajgenbaum (Every Cure / University of Pennsylvania); regimen administered by Coates's treating physician
segment: Individual off-label treatment of a terminal POEMS syndrome patient

ratings.reason: Coates had been told to choose between dying at home or in hospital and was too ill for a transplant. After the regimen he improved within a week and had a stem cell transplant about four months later. He was still in remission in the New York Times report of March 2025 and Every Cure's 2025 annual report.

ai_role.statement: Every Cure says an early version of its algorithms scored carfilzomib, cyclophosphamide, dexamethasone and related agents highly for POEMS syndrome. The reason was its similarity to multiple myeloma. The New York Times states the regimen was generated by an AI model rather than devised by a person. Fajgenbaum chose to query the platform, judged the output and relayed it. The treating doctor, who thought it sounded “a little bit crazy” per the New Yorker, administered three standard myeloma drugs. No clinical write-up of the case was found in PubMed or Europe PMC on 20 October 2026. Every Cure says a separate group described the same regimen for POEMS at a conference in summer 2024. So the drugs' plausibility does not rest on the model alone.

The page itself was not retrievable on 20 October 2026; its opening sentence was read on Every Cure's repost and its full text in Infobae's licensed Spanish edition.

headline: Every Cure's AI regimen puts a dying POEMS patient in remission
metric: he improved in a week and reached transplant and remission

comparator.against: the treatments his doctors had tried, with hospice as the remaining option
comparator.before: Coates was now entering a terminal stage: his heart and kidneys were failing, and fluid had to be drained from his belly several times a week. He was too sick to undergo a stem-cell transplant, which could save his life.
comparator.after: within days Coates started to improve. A few months later, he'd recovered sufficiently to receive a stem-cell transplant. He is now in remission.
comparator.quote: But, with little to lose, they gave it a try—and within days Coates started to improve. A few months later, he'd recovered sufficiently to receive a stem-cell transplant. He is now in remission.

later.note: Every Cure's 2025 annual report, created 7 January 2026 and posted on 16 January 2026, says that Joseph remains in remission; the New Yorker (15 July 2025) and Fajgenbaum's TED2025 talk also report him in remission and planning a wedding.
later.quote: Within a week, Joseph began improving. Four months later, he was healthy enough to receive a stem cell transplant. Today, he remains in remission — and makes the most of what he and Dr. Fajgenbaum call "overtime."
